newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani markets see mini-budget in offing.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani markets see mini-budget in offing.

text.p: Pakistani markets were braced on Thursday for Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto's cabinet to approve a possible mini-budget aimed at persuading the IMF to release delayed tranches of a $600 million standby loan.
Officials said a special cabinet meeting would take place on Thursday evening, but could not confirm that it would discuss a package proposed by the International Monetary Fund.
The government said last week that talks with the IMF in Washington had produced an understanding on the main elements of economic stabilisation and structural reforms.
It gave no details and senior officials involved in a flurry of top-level meetings have remained tight-lipped all week.

"It is believed that the government has been asked to impose an agriculture tax, reduce defence spending, cut non-development expenditure and reduce maximum customs duties to 55 percent," said stocks analyst Zuna Mansoor at ING Barings Securities.

The IMF has previously asked Pakistan to reduce its budget deficit to four percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in fiscal 1996/97 (July-June), from anywhere between an estimated five and six percent in the last fiscal year.
IMF concern has focused on Pakistan's vulnerable external position, given its large current account deficit and shrinking foreign reserves, now at about $900 million, excluding gold.
The IMF held back tranches of about $80 million each, due in June and September, amid doubts about Pakistan's implementation of agreed policies and confusion surrounding the 1996/97 budget.
It cannot disburse the delayed payments until a mission has visited Pakistan and completed a review of the economy.
Sources in the finance ministry said the IMF had made clear that it would not send a team to Islamabad until the government came up with a credible and comprehensive package.
Analysts say the absence of an IMF accord could send stock prices reeling and deter foreign lenders to Pakistan.
Satisfying the IMF, however, could pose an acute political challenge to Bhutto's three-year-old government, already under opposition fire for alleged corruption and mismanagement.
The scope for spending cuts is limited, given that defence and debt servicing swallow 55 percent of the budget.

"It now appears inevitable that Bhutto will have to take politically tough decisions in an attempt to get the economy back on track. However, all of the proposed measures are certain to arouse a strong reaction," Mansoor said.
Defence spending has previously been regarded as sacrosanct in view of Pakistan's long-running conflict with India.
Pakistan's big landowners, a politically dominant class known here as feudals, have thwarted attempts since 1993 to impose an effective agricultural income tax.

Local traders and businessmen strongly opposed a general sales tax imposed on imports and manufactures in the 1996/97 budget in June, forcing the government to make several concessions, which might now be withdrawn under IMF pressure.

"The government will have to comply (with IMF demands) no matter what," analyst Nauman Sheikh of Kasb & Co said, adding that Pakistan badly needed IMF support to restore investor confidence and avoid a possible cut in its credit ratings.
On September 23, the U.S.-based ratings agency Moody's Investors Service Inc put Pakistan's ratings under review for possible downgrade.
Dealer Dawar Hussain of Global Securities said the markets would view an IMF-inspired package as harsh but necessary.

"The markets will initially react negatively to measures affecting industry but eventually they will swallow the bitter pill if the measures bring IMF support and a positive response from credit ratings agencies," he said.
